text: The Rastriya Prajatantra Party (Nepali: राष्ट्रिय प्रजातन्त्र पार्टी, lit. 'National Democratic Party'; abbr. RPP, RaPraPa) is a constitutional monarchist and Hindu nationalist political party in Nepal. It was formed by Panchayat era prime ministers Surya Bahadur Thapa and Lokendra Bahadur Chand on 29 May 1990 by the ruling elite of that era. The party split in the same year when another group registered with the Election Commission, resulting in two parties with identical names, ideologies, and statutes but different flags and symbols. The two factions—led by Thapa and Chand—contested the 1991 elections, winning a total of four seats, with Chand’s party securing three and Thapa’s one. They agreed to merge into a single Rastriya Prajatantra Party on 8 February 1992. The party held its first general convention from 11 to 16 June 1992 in Kathmandu, where Surya Bahadur Thapa was unanimously elected chairman, with Lokendra Bahadur Chand and Rajeshwor Devkota elected leader and co-chairman, respectively. The party emerged as a third force in the 1992 local and 1994 general elections, receiving 18 percent of the votes and winning 20 seats, becoming the third-largest party in parliament. Initially supporting the CPN (UML) minority government, the party later withdrew support and backed a no-confidence motion against Manmohan Adhikari. It then joined a coalition government under Sher Bahadur Deuba with the Nepali Congress and Nepal Sadbhawana Party. In March 1996, a faction led by Chand saw cabinet ministers resign, but they withdrew before a no-confidence vote and Deuba won the confidence vote. In December 1996, six ministers again resigned but rejoined after supporting Deuba. In March 1997, a faction led by Chand joined a coalition with CPN (UML), with Chand as prime minister. On 3 October 1997, Thapa’s faction voted for a no-confidence motion, leading to Thapa becoming prime minister on 6 October 1997 with Congress support. After losing party support, Thapa asked King Birendra to dissolve parliament and call fresh elections. The Supreme Court recommended the session, and Thapa survived the no-confidence vote, expelling six central committee members for threatening to back the motion. The party’s second general convention took place from 12 to 16 November 1997 in Birgunj, re-electing Thapa as chairman. Prakash Chandra Lohani, Pashupati SJB Rana, and Kamal Thapa were elected vice-chairman, general secretary, and spokesman, respectively. On 9 January 1998, Lokendra Bahadur Chand created a separate Rastriya Prajatantra Party, accusing Thapa of mismanagement and unfair elections, and broke away with 10 MPs, including 8 from the House of Representatives and 2 from the National Assembly. Thapa resigned as prime minister on 10 April 1998 and was replaced by Girija Prasad Koirala. In the 1999 elections, the party won 11 seats and Chand’s faction won none. The parties merged again on 31 December 1999, but a group led by Rajeshwor Devkota formed their own Rastriya Prajatantra Party (Nationalist). King Gyanendra dismissed Sher Bahadur Deuba’s government on 4 October 2002 after failing to conduct elections following the dissolution of the House of Representatives in May 2002. Lokendra Bahadur Chand was appointed prime minister on 11 October 2002 and resigned on 31 May 2003 due to protests demanding a national consensus government and restoration of parliament; he was replaced by Surya Bahadur Thapa on 5 June 2002. At the third general convention in Pokhara from 12 to 14 December 2002, Thapa completed his second four-year term as chairman and could not run again per party constitution. Pashupati Shamsher Jang Bahadur Rana was elected chairman, with Padma Sundar Lawati, Kamal Thapa, and Rosan Karki nominated as vice-president, general secretary, and spokesperson. There were calls within the party for Thapa to resign for undermining democracy by failing to form a national consensus government; he resigned on 7 May 2004 and was replaced by Sher Bahadur Deuba. On 4 November 2004, Thapa announced he would quit the party to form a new centre-right liberal party, launched as the Rastriya Janashakti Party on 13 March 2005. On 1 February 2005, King Gyanendra dismissed Deuba and seized executive powers. The party supported the pro-democracy agitation led by the Seven Party Alliance, though ten central committee members, including Kamal Thapa, supported the coup. Thapa and six central committee members were appointed to the King’s cabinet in December 2005, with Thapa becoming Home Minister. On 10 January 2006, members close to Kamal Thapa voted to replace Pashupati Shamsher Jang Bahadur Rana as chairman with Thapa, but the claim was dismissed. Thapa’s faction contested the 2006 local elections, boycotted by the Seven Party Alliance and the Rana faction, and won mayoral positions in Kathmandu, Pokhara, Bharatpur, and Dhangadhi amid low turnout, violence, and lack of candidates. Six incumbent cabinet ministers supporting Thapa were expelled, and on 28 October 2006, they formed the royalist Rastriya Prajatantra Party Nepal under Kamal Thapa. The party held its fourth general convention from 9 to 11 December 2007, re-electing Pashupati SJB Rana as chairman. After the 2006 revolution, a national consensus government under Girija Prasad Koirala was formed, and parliament was reinstated and transformed into the Interim Legislature Parliament after including the Maoists. The party had eight seats, but two MPs, Budhhiman Tamang and Brijesh Kumar Gupta, were dismissed for supporting the royal coup. In the 2008 elections, the party failed to win a constituency seat but received 2.45% of party list votes and won 8 seats in the 1st Constituent Assembly through proportional representation. Party chairman Pashupati SJB Rana lost in Sindhupalchowk 1. At the first session of the 1st Constituent Assembly on 28 May 2008, the party voted to abolish the monarchy and establish a republic. Lokendra Bahadur Chand, the parliamentary party leader, was absent. The party joined the Madhav Kumar Nepal-led government in June 2009. At the fifth general convention from 17 to 19 May 2013, the Rastriya Janashakti Party merged into the RPP, and Surya Bahadur Thapa was elected chairman. It was decided that senior leadership would rotate annually among Thapa, Chand, Rana, and Prakash Chandra Lohani. In the 2013 elections, the party won constituency seats in Rupandehi 2, Chitwan 5, and Dhankuta 2, received 2.75% of party list votes, and won 10 proportional seats for a total of 13 seats in the 2nd Constituent Assembly. The party supported the CPN (UML)-Nepali Congress coalition under Sushil Koirala and sent two ministers to the cabinet. On 21 November 2016, the party unified with the Kamal Thapa-led Rastriya Prajatantra Party Nepal, retaining the name Rastriya Prajatantra Party. The unified party had 37 members in parliament, becoming the fourth-largest party. Thapa was elected chairman in a special general convention in Kathmandu in February 2017. The party joined the coalition government on 9 March 2017 under CPN (Maoist Centre) leader Pushpa Kamal Dahal, with Kamal Thapa serving as deputy prime minister. Prakash Chandra Lohani split from the party over the coalition decision and electoral symbol issues, forming the Ekikrit Rastriya Prajatantra Party (Nationalist) on 29 March 2017. On 6 August 2017, Pashupati SJB Rana broke away to form the Rastriya Prajatantra Party (Democratic). The party joined the coalition under Sher Bahadur Deuba on 13 October 2017 with Kamal Thapa again as deputy prime minister. In the 2017 general and provincial elections, the party formed an alliance with the Nepali Congress and Rastriya Prajatantra Party (Democratic). It won only one seat in the House of Representatives, with party chairman Kamal Thapa losing in Makwanpur 1. Only general secretary Rajendra Lingden was elected from Jhapa 3 after forging an electoral pact with the Left Alliance in eastern districts. The party received 2.06% of party list votes, failing to pass the 3% threshold and thus not becoming a national party. It won one seat each in provincial assemblies of Province 1, Province 3, and Province 6. The Rastriya Prajatantra Party (Samyukta), formed from the merger of Rana and Lohani’s splinter groups, merged with the party on 12 March 2020, with Kamal Thapa, Rana, and Lohani all acting as chairs. On 1 July 2020, Sunil Bahadur Thapa, son of Surya Bahadur Thapa, resigned and joined the Nepali Congress. The party held its general convention from 1 to 3 December 2021 and elected Rajendra Prasad Lingden as chairman, defeating incumbent chairman Kamal Thapa. The party announced it had 150,000 active members. The convention also elected Nepalgunj mayor Dhawal Shamsher Rana as general secretary and former member of the constituent assembly Bikram Pandey as vice-president. Following the convention, Kamal Thapa left the party and revived the Rastriya Prajatantra Party Nepal. The party announced plans to unify pro-monarchist groups, including Nepal Ka Lagi Nepali Campaign, Mission Nepal, Gorach Abhiyan, and the Gyanendra Shahi-led Hamro Nepal Hami Nepali Campaign, with these groups joining in the following months. Former chairman of Bibeksheel Sajha Party, Rabindra Mishra, joined on 28 September 2022 as senior vice-president. The Janatantrik Terai Mukti Morcha merged with the party on 5 October. The party fielded 140 candidates in the 2022 general and provincial elections and forged an electoral pact with CPN (UML) in Jhapa, Banke, and Rupandehi districts. Party chairman Rajendra Lingden retained his seat in Jhapa 3 and the party gained six additional direct seats. It received 5.58% of party list votes, becoming one of seven national parties in the Federal Parliament, and won seven proportional seats for a total of 14 seats in the House of Representatives. The party also won seats in all seven provincial assemblies. The party joined the coalition government of Pushpa Kamal Dahal following the election, with three cabinet ministers and one state minister, and party president Lingden serving as deputy prime minister. It withdrew from the coalition after one month. The party was established as an alternative to the major parties, the Nepali Congress and CPN (UML), founded on principles of democracy, constitutional monarchy, nationalism, and economic liberalism. At its founding, Thapa’s party was seen as more liberal and Chand’s as more conservative. At the first session of the 1st Constituent Assembly, the party voted to abolish the monarchy and establish a secular republic. Later, it advocated for a Hindu republic. The splinter group Rastriya Prajatantra Party Nepal, which had voted against abolishing the monarchy, changed its constitution to support a Hindu state and return to constitutional monarchy. After the 2016 merger, the unified party adopted the constitution of Rastriya Prajatantra Party Nepal. The party has supported a Sanatan Hindu state with full religious freedom and submitted an amendment proposal on 19 March 2017. The Election Commission removed provisions advocating a Hindu state and monarchy on 17 March 2017 and asked the party to remove them again on 22 January 2022, citing violation of Article 260 of the Constitution of Nepal. The party supports a ceremonial monarch, a directly elected prime minister, and a fully proportional parliament. It also calls for scrapping provincial governments, calling them an expensive experiment, and instead advocates strengthening local governments and creating a two-tier federal structure.

The Rastriya Prajatantra Party Nepal, a splinter group that originally opposed the abolition of the monarchy, amended its constitution to advocate for the re-establishment of a Sanatan Hindu state and a return to a constitutional monarchy. Following the merger between the two parties in November 2016, the unified party adopted the constitution of Rastriya Prajatantra Party Nepal. The party has publicly supported a Sanatan Hindu state with full religious freedom and submitted an amendment proposal for this on 19 March 2017. On 17 March 2017, the Election Commission removed the section of the party's statute promoting a Hindu state and monarchy, and later, on 22 January 2022, requested the party to remove these provisions again, citing a violation of Article 260 of the Constitution of Nepal. The party supports a ceremonial monarch, a directly elected prime minister, and a fully proportional parliament. It also calls for the abolition of provincial governments, describing them as an expensive experiment, and instead advocates for strengthening local governments and establishing a two-tier federal structure.
